rv.q: But there is craft in Omar Elerian’s direction, which builds intrigue while keeping an air of improvisation. The two actors play out flashes of Brunner’s life – as a gruff figure in hospital, or an irascible old man railing against Lenin and democracy in a video rental shop – but they weave this with the story of their vanished writer.
The Long Shadow of Alois Brunner completely avoids that.
I found that the story lacked structure, and ended up being difficult to follow in places.
